title: Candidates, cost and ergonomics
goal: Know which words get a stroke, which strokes are reserved before any word, every source of candidate outlines, the one formula that ranks them, and how the ergonomic term scores finger shape.

blocks.x: Who counts as a word

`ranked_words` takes the frequency list's top 100,000 that have a pronunciation, in plain lowercase (letters and apostrophes only). Two kinds of token are dropped because they were frequency-list artifacts claiming short strokes they could never use.

items: **The bare letter "i".** The list spells the pronoun lowercase, so the letter would inherit the pronoun's count. The pronoun keeps its own entry on [[I|EU]]; the letter is fingerspelled. `a` is the only single-letter word.

**Contraction tails** (`'s 'd 'll 're 'm 've 't 'n 'a`). The tokenizer splits "I've" into "i" + "'ve", so each tail would carry a whole contraction family's count. Struck alone it would type the tail with its space. The strokes they would have held go to real words: [[guess|ES]], [[you'll|UL]], [[um|UPL]], [[tour|TUR]]. Clipped words that are real on their own (`'cause`, `'em`, `'til`) stay.

The candidate pool

`enumerate_candidates` is a pure function: given a word it returns every legal outline, tagged with where it came from, and touches no shared state. The pool is built across every core (`enumerate_in_parallel`) with a byte-identical result. No candidate is preferred by construction; the solver settles that later, on cost. Candidates that land on the same rendered text are deduplicated, keeping the cheaper one.

blocks.x: A short form never takes a stroke the plain rules already give

items: A brevity step (and its first two star rungs) is dropped if some word's plain rules already give that text. Every outline a learner could work out by the rules stays that word's.

A short form that lands on the starred stroke of a one-syllable rules stroke pays `STAR_SURCHARGE` (12,500, which is half a stroke) on top of its cost. A star on a one-syllable stroke means its sound-alike: [[dock|TKO*BG]] and [[sock|SO*BG]] carry the star, [[doc|TKOBG]] does not.
The surcharge is a price, not a ban. A short form that would otherwise cost a whole extra stroke, for a word much commoner than the sound-alike, still takes it: [[attack|TA*BG]] keeps its star.

blocks.x: The cost formula
`candidate_cost` is intrinsic to the outline alone. It knows nothing about the word, how often it is said, or any other word's candidates. Every candidate from every source is reduced to one number.

head: Tier
Weight
Why it ranks there
rows: A stroke costs 25 keys and one stroke holds at most 24, so a one-stroke outline always costs less than any two-stroke outline: no word prefers a longer outline for itself.
Counts how many keys, not which.
Stays under 1,000 even for every key at once (`*` included, which scores 928), so it only breaks ties between candidates with the same strokes and keys. It is the only tier that knows which keys.

Where frequency enters
Frequency is not in the formula above. The solver multiplies a candidate's cost by how often the word is said (its count in the frequency corpus), one level up:
edge_cost(word, candidate) = weight(word) x candidate_cost(candidate.outline)

Minimizing the sum of `edge_cost` over every word is the whole objective, and it is the same metric `!build` reports as keys per word weighted by how often it is said. For one word, frequency changes nothing about which of its own candidates is best. It only decides who wins when two words want the same text.
Why a stroke weighs 25 keys

25 is the smallest round number above the 24 keys one stroke can hold, so the per-word order is fixed; only cross-word trades move. The weight is finite on purpose: once frequency is multiplied in, one extra stroke for a rare word is weighed against extra keys for a common one instead of always winning. A cross-word trade can also go the other way: a rare word may be written with a longer form so that a commoner word holds the one-stroke form.
Ergonomics: what costly means at the finger level

Two outlines can tie on strokes and keys and still feel different to type. [[TK]], one finger pressing both of its own rows, is effortless. [[STWH]], four fingers alternating top and bottom, is not, although it is also one stroke and four keys. `src/ergonomics.rs` tells those apart. Every number in it traces to the keyboard geometry keymux presses or to a finger-biomechanics measurement (Häger-Ross and Schieber, J Neurosci 2000).
Every key is a reach vector
Each key is a `(vertical, lateral)` reach, each axis 0 (the finger's own row) or 1 (one key away), checked key by key against the QWERTY layout keymux presses.

items: The right pinky's `D` and `Z` pair uses the stretch column.

The right index's `*` is struck via `H` (home, lateral) or `Y` (top, lateral). `*` folds into the right index's own column as a wildcard: it fills whichever of `F` or `R` is not in use, so `*` plus `F` costs no more than a same-finger double press.
These two are the only digits asked to reach a second position; that overload is priced by how far the reach is, through its vector, not by a flat tax.

blocks.x: Two measurements: the ring finger struggles most

Häger-Ross and Schieber measured two indices per finger. **Individuation (II)** is how independently a finger moves to its own target while its neighbors move to theirs: the right quantity for two active fingers (a transition). **Stationarity (SI)** is how still a finger stays while its neighbors move: the right quantity for a finger held out of the way between two active ones (a gap). On both, the ring finger is the least independent, not the pinky.

Self-paced, averaged across the paper's left and right hand columns, times 1000. The deficit from 1.0 is the meaningful quantity; ring's `TRANS` is about 4.5 times index's. On the left hand the digit order is reversed (little, ring, middle, index); on the right it is index, middle, ring, little.
The four terms a stroke is scored on

head: Term
What it measures
Formula
rows: Walking a hand's active fingers in order, charging for how far two neighbors' reach vectors differ.
`(dv^2 + dl^2) x (TRANS[i] + TRANS[j])` for each pair of consecutively active fingers; zero when both reach the same way.
With two or more fingers active on a hand, each one's distance from rest.
`(v + l) x TRANS[finger]`; zero below two active fingers, so a same-finger double stays free.
A finger skipped between two active neighbors on the same hand.
A small flat cost per pinky key press, for leverage.
`PINKY_TAX` = 5 per press (`S-` on the left; `T`, `S`, `D`, `Z` on the right). Excludes the join key.

items: A same-finger double press is charged +1 in total and nothing else.
Squaring the per-axis difference makes transitions convex: asking two poorly coupled fingers to each reach further costs much more than twice a small reach.
The join key is excluded from every term: it appears in nearly every continuation stroke, so costing it would penalize "more than one stroke", not any real word choice.

`PINKY_TAX` is a judgment call, not a measurement. It is small relative to every other term (smaller than the smallest nonzero engagement cost, 56), so it can only break a tie between candidates that differ in pinky presses.
